answers.label: Benefits and challenges of consequential methods
answers.text: The Actions and Market Instruments (AMI) Technical Working Group (TWG) is currently producing a white paper, expected to be released during the current public consultation period, that will cover key concepts, principles, and approaches. For the GHG Protocol (GHGP) to benefit the most from stakeholder input, it is critical that such input be fully informed. The fact that stakeholders will not have an opportunity to consider the white paper as part of the Electricity-Sector Consequential Methods consultation period will limit stakeholders’ ability to provide fully informed comments and input. Developing consequential accounting methods for electricity-sector actions based on stakeholder feedback that is inadequately informed is likely to result in GHG reporting standards that do not accomplish the objectives of the program.

answers.label: Appropriateness of the TWG subgroup formula
Why the formula is or is not appropriate
answers.text:
The formula for quantifying emissions impacts from electricity projects should be kept as simple as possible initially. When calculating emissions impacts via the proposed formula, reporting entities should be allowed to use broad temporal level data and grid level data to simplify the accounting and estimating of emissions reductions from the project/program. Requiring data for calculations that is too granular at the beginning of the program risks making the accounting too complex and costly and could impact the project’s financial viability.

It would be more appropriate and workable for the formula to be refined over time as additional experience is gained with the new reporting guidelines.

answers.label: Why secondary effects should be excluded
answers.text:
Reporters should not have to consider secondary effects in addition to primary effects when quantifying the emissions impacts from electricity projects. The formula for quantifying emissions impacts from electricity projects should be kept as simple as possible initially to avoid unnecessary complexities. Since stakeholders are being deprived of decision-important information, as referred to in EEI’s response to question 18 above, reporters should only have to address primary effects to mitigate complexity.

If it becomes appropriate over time, the formula could be refined as additional experience is gained with the new reporting guidelines.

answers.label: Requiredness of the financial analysis test
Requiredness of the common practice test
Why selected tests should be included
answers.text:
Each of the provided additionality tests should be included as optional in a proposed framework designed to assess additionality for renewable energy projects. The framework should only require the actual application of a limited number (e.g., two) of additionality tests for renewable energy projects. The use of additionality should be applied in a limited fashion. When assessing additionality for renewable energy projects, care must be taken to ensure that its application in a forward-looking context is done in a straightforward manner and not subjectively.

Further, the Protocol must consider that some reporters already are required to apply certain additionality tests for mandatory compliance with other programs, (such as European Union (EU) requirements), while other reporters may apply additionality tests wholly voluntarily. Hence, for the purposes of the Protocol, reporters should be allowed to select which additionality tests are applied to their projects. Doing so also will allow reporters the flexibility to consider company-specific and regional circumstances in selecting which tests are appropriate for each project.

Consequential accounting requirements, including additionality tests, should be no more stringent than those of the federal or state reporting program for off-system reductions that a reporter may be complying with. The Protocol should recognize the emissions reductions of a renewable energy project if it is in compliance with reporting guidelines under a federal or state reporting program, including any additionality tests that a reporting entity is subject to under such guidelines.

Allowing flexibility in the application of additionality tests for renewable energy projects will help ensure the continued development and deployment of needed energy infrastructure and avoid undue burdens where additionality tests are not required for mandatory compliance.

answers.label: Context on test feasibility
answers.text: The feasibility of implementing any given additionality test can be determined only by the reporter and only on a project-by-project basis. By definition, what is feasible will vary by reporter. This is because there are a number of considerations, a few of which are noted in EEI’s response to question 27 above, required in determining which additionality tests are feasible for their projects and the conclusions will differ from company to company. Because of such variability, the Protocol should allow for flexibility in the methods of assessing additionality.

answers.label: Additionality tests missing from the framework
answers.text: If any additionality tests not already included in the guidance materials emerge and are subsequently included in a proposed framework designed to assess additionality for renewable energy projects, such tests must be optional. Stakeholders would not have had the opportunity to review and comment on such tests, and thus their inclusion would not be the result of a fully informed process.

answers.label: Regions warranting different tests, with examples
answers.text: The Protocol must allow flexibility for the consideration of regional differences in additionality tests. Regional differences will present unique considerations for determining the appropriate additionality tests, as noted in EEI’s response to question 27 above.

answers.label: Details on operating margin methodologies
answers.text: Given the significant complexity of these methodologies, EEI is not in a position to fully analyze them or provide in‑depth feedback at this time. Also, systems applying these methodologies are still under development and different approaches may be found in the future, such as through the application of artificial intelligence (AI). Because of this, the use of operating margin emission rates would benefit from a more extensive public consultation process.

answers.label: Details on build margin methodologies
answers.text: As noted in EEI’s response to question 37 above, EEI is not in a position to fully analyze these methodologies or provide in‑depth feedback at this time, and the use of build margin emission rates would benefit from a more extensive public consultation process.

answers.label: Why that spatial granularity ceiling
answers.text: The country is the maximum appropriate level of spatial granularity for marginal emission rates. Per the tables depicting OMER and BMER datasets on pages 14 and 15 of this public consultation document, Consequential Electricity-Sector Emissions Impacts, many OMER and BMER datasets used apply the country as their level of spatial granularity. As the tables demonstrate, each methodological approach may be applied using different levels of spatial granularity; therefore, the broadest level of spatial granularity should be considered appropriate according to the datasets.

answers.label: Why that temporal granularity ceiling
answers.text:
Annual data is the maximum appropriate level of temporal granularity for marginal emission rates. As described in EEI’s response to question 44 above, many OMER and BMER datasets apply annual data as their level of temporal granularity and each methodological approach may be applied using different levels of temporal granularity. As such, the broadest level of temporal granularity should be considered appropriate according to the datasets.

Narrower levels of temporal granularity, such as hourly tracking, is no guarantee of higher accuracy in data and such data may not be available for many reporting entities. For example, MISO’s new live hourly dashboard does not account for battery storage in their datasets, skewing the marginal emission rates.

answers.label: Why selected weighting approaches are appropriate
answers.text: Reiterating from section 8.3, EEI is not in a position to provide more in-depth feedback at this time, and build and operating margin weighting should be examined under a more extensive public consultation process.

answers.label: Weighting approaches not feasible to implement
Why selected weighting approaches are infeasible
answers.text: Reiterating from section 8.3, EEI is not in a position to provide more in-depth feedback at this time, and build and operating margin weighting should be examined under a more extensive public consultation process.
